🍋 Partial Fulfillment — lamps and wicks, an etrog and a pomegranate, a robe and a cloak

overview.title: 📖 Overview: The Fine Grain of Agency Law
overview.subtitle: Meilah 21a–21b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf works through an escalating series of agency scenarios to pin down exactly when the homeowner or the agent bears liability for me'ilah. A literal instruction, obeyed literally, binds the homeowner even if his unspoken intent differed — 'matters of the heart are not matters.' Sending consecrated funds through someone legally incapable of agency (a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor) still works, through a creative comparison to olives releasing beneficial moisture. The daf then walks through cases of partial fulfillment — half the instructions followed, half not — testing when both parties, one party, or neither becomes liable, and closes with a mishna on money deposited with a money changer versus a homeowner, and the classic dispute between Rabbi Akiva and the Rabbis over a stray consecrated coin lost in one's purse.

slides.title: 🗣️ Literal Words Win Over Silent Intent
slides.subtitle: The window-or-chest case
rows: 'Bring it from the window OR the chest' (either is fine)
Agent brought it from the chest; homeowner secretly wanted the window
The HOMEOWNER — his stated instruction was fulfilled; silent intent doesn't count
'Bring it specifically from the window'
Agent brought it from the chest instead
The AGENT — he deviated from a specific instruction
'Bring it specifically from the chest'
Agent brought it from the window instead
The AGENT — same principle, reversed

callout.label: The lesson (Gemara):
callout.text: 'דְּבָרִים שֶׁבַּלֵּב אֵינָם דְּבָרִים' — unspoken preferences carry no legal weight. Only the words actually spoken define the agency's terms.

slides.title: 🐒 Can People Who Can't Be Agents Still Act as Agents?
slides.subtitle: Explaining how a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor can still trigger the homeowner's liability

nodes.content: ❓ A deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor legally CANNOT be formally appointed as an agent — so how can sending consecrated money through them make the HOMEOWNER liable when they succeed?

🫒 Rabbi Elazar: like the olive-press vat, where beneficial moisture is treated as occurring with the owner's 'intent' simply because it serves his purpose — so too here, since the outcome suits the homeowner, it's treated as his own act
🐘 Rabbi Yoḥanan's parallel: like placing an eiruv on a monkey or trained elephant that carries it to the right spot — the animal 'performs' the agency though it cannot legally be an agent
✅ Either way: successful, purpose-serving completion of the task is enough to attribute the result to the homeowner — legal agency isn't strictly required

slides.title: 🍋 Partial Fulfillment: Who's Liable for What?
slides.subtitle: Half-instructions, split purchases, and Rabbi Yehuda's dissent
rows: Half a peruta for lamps, half for wicks
All lamps, or all wicks
NEITHER liable — instructions followed for only half a peruta each way
All of a peruta for lamps (or wicks) from ONE place each
Lamps from the wick-place, wicks from the lamp-place
The AGENT is liable — deviated on the full peruta
Two perutot: 'bring me an etrog'
An etrog with one peruta, a pomegranate with the other
BOTH liable — homeowner for the etrog peruta, agent for the pomegranate peruta. Rabbi Yehuda dissents: homeowner isn't liable, since he can say 'I wanted a BIGGER etrog'
A gold dinar: 'bring me a robe'
A robe (3 sela) plus a cloak (3 sela)
BOTH liable — same logic. Rabbi Yehuda again exempts the homeowner: 'I wanted a finer robe for the full price'

callout.label: Gemara's clarification:
callout.text: Rabbi Yehuda's defense works because the agent found a genuine bargain — had he spent the FULL amount as instructed, the homeowner would have gotten an even better item, so the homeowner can plausibly claim dissatisfaction rather than acceptance.

slides.title: 🏦 New Mishna: Money Changer vs. Homeowner
slides.subtitle: Who may use deposited consecrated money — and where does a storekeeper fit?

boxes.title: Money Changer (Bound coins)
items: If he spends them: liable for me'ilah

boxes.title: Money Changer (Loose/unbound coins)
items: If he spends them: NOT liable

boxes.title: Ordinary Homeowner (either way)
items: May NEVER use deposited funds, bound or not
If he spends them: always liable

callout.label: Where does the storekeeper fit?
callout.text: Rabbi Meir: a storekeeper is treated like an ordinary HOMEOWNER — never permitted to use deposits. Rabbi Yehuda: a storekeeper is treated like a MONEY CHANGER — permitted to use loose coins, since storekeepers commonly handle cash the way money changers do.

slides.title: 🪙 A Stray Consecrated Peruta in the Purse
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Akiva vs. the Rabbis, and a subtle wording difference

lines.speaker: Rabbi Akiva
lines.text: If a consecrated peruta fell into an ordinary purse — or someone said 'a peruta IN this purse is consecrated' — once the FIRST peruta is spent, he's liable, since any coin might be the consecrated one.

lines.speaker: Rabbis
lines.text: Not liable until he spends the ENTIRE purse — only then is it certain the consecrated peruta was actually spent.

lines.speaker: But Rabbi Akiva concedes...
lines.text: If someone said 'a peruta FROM this purse is consecrated' — everyone agrees: not liable until the WHOLE purse is spent.

lines.speaker: Rabbi Yoḥanan's resolution
lines.text: The wording shift matters: 'from this purse' implies he meant 'let this purse not be exempt from consecration' — i.e., his intent was for the VERY LAST coin to be the consecrated one, so only spending everything triggers liability.

summary.principle: Agency for me'ilah is defined by spoken instructions rather than private intent, extends even through legally incapable messengers when the outcome serves the sender's purpose, and every partial fulfillment, deposit arrangement, or ambiguous wording is resolved by asking precisely what was said and precisely what happened.

flowSteps.content: 🗣️ Spoken instructions bind; silent intent does not — 'matters of the heart are not matters'
🐒 Even a legally incompetent messenger's success is attributed to the homeowner, per the olive-vat and eiruv-animal analogies
🍋 Partial fulfillment splits liability precisely along the lines of what was and wasn't followed

columns.content: 🏦 Money changers may use loose deposits; homeowners never may; storekeepers are disputed
🪙 'A peruta IN this purse' vs. 'FROM this purse' yields opposite liability timing

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: precision in wording and precision in action together determine exactly who bears responsibility for misuse

quiz.q: According to the mishna, if a homeowner tells an agent 'bring it from the window or the chest' (either is acceptable) and the agent brings it from the chest despite the homeowner's silent preference for the window, who is liable for me'ilah?
o: The agent, since he didn't guess the homeowner's true wish
The homeowner, since 'matters of the heart are not matters' — only the spoken instruction counts
Neither party is liable
Both parties share liability equally
quiz.e: The Gemara explains that unspoken intentions carry no legal weight; since the agent fulfilled the literal spoken instruction, the homeowner bears the liability.

quiz.q: How does Rabbi Elazar explain that sending consecrated money through a deaf-mute, imbecile, or minor can still create liability for the homeowner, despite these individuals being legally incapable of formal agency?
o: He says the mishna is incorrect

He compares it to olives in a press-vat, where beneficial moisture is treated as occurring with the owner's intent simply because it serves his purpose — similarly, a successful outcome is attributed to the homeowner
He says only adults can ever be considered agents, so the ruling doesn't really apply
He says these individuals are actually legally competent for this purpose
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar's analogy teaches that when an outcome serves the owner's purpose, it can be treated as though done with his intent, even without formal legal agency.

quiz.q: In the case of a homeowner giving an agent two perutot for an etrog, but the agent buying an etrog with one and a pomegranate with the other, what is Rabbi Yehuda's dissenting view?
o: That neither party is liable at all
That the homeowner is NOT liable, since he can claim he wanted a larger, better etrog worth the full two perutot, and thus didn't get what he wanted
That only the pomegranate seller is liable
That the agent is exempt in this case
quiz.e: Rabbi Yehuda argues the homeowner can plausibly say he wanted a superior etrog for the full amount, meaning his instructions weren't truly fulfilled, so he shouldn't be liable.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, what is the difference between a money changer and an ordinary homeowner regarding deposited consecrated money?
o: There is no difference between them
A money changer may use LOOSE (unbound) deposited coins, while an ordinary homeowner may never use deposited money, bound or unbound
A homeowner may always use deposited money freely
A money changer may never use any deposited money
quiz.e: The mishna distinguishes a money changer, who may use unbound coins (since that's the nature of his business), from a homeowner, who is never permitted to use deposited funds under any circumstances.

quiz.q: What is the key difference between saying 'a peruta IN this purse is consecrated' versus 'a peruta FROM this purse is consecrated,' according to Rabbi Yoḥanan's resolution?
o: There is no difference; both phrasings yield identical rulings

'In this purse' triggers liability upon spending the FIRST coin (Rabbi Akiva); 'from this purse' means the LAST coin was intended as consecrated, so liability begins only once the entire purse is spent
'From this purse' means no coins are ever consecrated
Both phrasings exempt the person from all liability
quiz.e: Rabbi Yoḥanan explains that 'from this purse' implies the person meant the purse should not be exempted from consecration until the very end, meaning the final remaining coin was intended as the consecrated one.
